english.html: r to the said Martin, and having heard from him (under pretext of friendship) several private and particular things about him and about his wife.

One of the most singular fruits and most precious effects of friendship is the sweetness and the pleasure one has in being able freely to disclose one's secrets and one's thoughts to one's friend, who is another self. Is there anything in the world more singular (says Cicero somewhere) than to have a man with whom you can, and dare, speak as to yourself <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, and by whom, said Plautus, you will never be deceived <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>.

notes.original: Ciceron en ſon liure de l'amitiê.
notes.gloss: "What is sweeter than to have someone with whom you may dare to speak of everything as with yourself?"

notes.citation: Plautus, Poenulus, as Coras cites it; the distich has not been located in the play
notes.original: Plaute en la comedie inſcripte, Pœnulus.

english.html: No one is deceived, in my opinion at least, who tells his affairs frankly to his friends (Decipitur nemo, mea quidem sententia, / qui suis amicis narrat recte res suas).

O what a great good it is (added Seneca) when hearts are so well prepared that every secret descends into them in safety: whose conscience you fear less than your own; whose talk removes and calms the disquiet of your mind, whose opinion gives you counsel, and whose sight rejoices and consoles you <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. Certainly the happiness and good is so great that Socrates and Darius said that all the lands and goods of this world cannot be compared with a good, true and prudent friend. Alexander the Great, passing by Troy, crowned the statue of Achilles, and praised him as fortunate in nothing so much as in having had Patroclus for a friend. O happy Achilles (said he), who had in your life so loyal and entire a friend as Patroclus <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. True it is that such and so perfect friends as an Achilles and Patroclus, a Pylades and Orestes, a Damon and Pythias, a Theseus and Pirithous, are not to be found today, so unhappy is our age.

notes.original: Seneca ou liure de la trãquillite de la vie.
notes.gloss: Quantum bonum est, ubi sunt praeparata pectora in quae tuto secretum omne descendat … — Coras translates the passage closely.
Alexander at Troy garlands the tomb of Achilles and calls him happy for having had a faithful friend in life and a great herald after death; Coras makes it a statue.

english.html: That once venerable name of friendship is prostituted, and sits for hire like a harlot. No one is loved unless fortune favours him;
